q: Set up a project in /home/ansible/project: a config file making that directory self-contained, an inventory with a webservers group (web1, web2) and a dbservers group (db1), both inside a production group, and privilege escalation on by default. Prove connectivity.
a:
**`/home/ansible/project/ansible.cfg`:**

```ini
[defaults]
inventory        = ./inventory
remote_user      = ansible
host_key_checking = False
roles_path       = ./roles
collections_path = ./collections

[privilege_escalation]
become        = True
become_method = sudo
become_user   = root
become_ask_pass = False
```

**`/home/ansible/project/inventory`:**

```ini
[webservers]
web1.example.com
web2.example.com

[dbservers]
db1.example.com

[production:children]
webservers
dbservers
```

**Verify — all four of these, in order:**

```bash
cd /home/ansible/project
ansible --version                 # confirms WHICH ansible.cfg is in effect
ansible-inventory --graph         # the tree, including production's children
ansible all --list-hosts          # three hosts
ansible all -m ping               # pong from each
```

**If the config seems ignored**, two causes: you're not in the project directory (`./ansible.cfg` is only found from there), or the directory is **world-writable**, which makes Ansible refuse to load it. `ansible --version` names the file it actually used, which settles it immediately.

**If ping fails**, run `ansible all -m ping -vvv` — it prints the exact SSH command, which usually makes the problem obvious (wrong user, missing key, unknown host).

q: Every host in webservers should use http_port: 8080, except web2.example.com, which must use 9090. Don't put either value in a playbook.
a:
Use the auto-loaded variable directories next to the inventory:

```bash
mkdir -p group_vars host_vars
```

```yaml
# group_vars/webservers.yml
---
http_port: 8080
```

```yaml
# host_vars/web2.example.com.yml
---
http_port: 9090
```

**Verify without writing a playbook:**

```bash
ansible webservers -m ansible.builtin.debug -a "var=http_port"
# web1 -> 8080
# web2 -> 9090
```

**Why this works:** host variables have **higher precedence** than group variables, so `web2`'s file wins for that host only, and no conditional logic is needed anywhere. If you ever need to override both from the command line, `-e http_port=1234` beats everything — which is also the thing to check if a value mysteriously isn't what your files say.

q: Write /home/ansible/project/webserver.yml: install httpd on webservers, enable and start it, open the firewall for the http service, and deploy an index.html showing the host's own fully-qualified domain name. It must be idempotent.
a:
**`templates/index.html.j2`:** ```jinja

Welcome to {{ ansible_facts['fqdn'] }}

``` **`webserver.yml`:** ```yaml --- - name: Configure web servers hosts: webservers become: true tasks: - name: Install httpd and firewalld ansible.builtin.dnf: name: - httpd - firewalld state: present - name: Start and enable firewalld ansible.builtin.service: name: firewalld state: started enabled: true - name: Open the http service ansible.posix.firewalld: service: http state: enabled permanent: true immediate: true - name: Deploy the home page ansible.builtin.template: src: index.html.j2 dest: /var/www/html/index.html owner: root group: root mode: '0644' notify: Restart httpd - name: Start and enable httpd ansible.builtin.service: name: httpd state: started enabled: true handlers: - name: Restart httpd ansible.builtin.service: name: httpd state: restarted ``` **Verify:** ```bash ansible-playbook webserver.yml # first run: changes ansible-playbook webserver.yml # SECOND run: changed=0 <- the real test ansible webservers -m ansible.builtin.uri -a "url=http://localhost/ return_content=true" ``` **The details that earn the marks.** `permanent: true` *and* `immediate: true` together (permanent alone doesn't affect the running firewall). `state: present` rather than `latest`, so re-runs stay clean. `notify:` on the template, so httpd restarts only where the page actually changed. And `ansible_facts['fqdn']` in the template rather than a hardcoded name — that's the clause making this a template task instead of a copy task.

q: Create users from a variable containing a list of dictionaries: each has a name and a group. Users in the devs group get a bash shell; others get /sbin/nologin. The groups must exist first.
a:
```yaml
# group_vars/all.yml
---
users:
  - name: ana
    group: devs
  - name: raj
    group: devs
  - name: svcbot
    group: services
```

```yaml
---
- name: Manage users
  hosts: all
  become: true

  tasks:
    - name: Ensure groups exist
      ansible.builtin.group:
        name: "{{ item }}"
        state: present
      loop: "{{ users | map(attribute='group') | unique | list }}"

    - name: Create users
      ansible.builtin.user:
        name: "{{ item.name }}"
        groups: "{{ item.group }}"
        append: true
        shell: "{{ '/bin/bash' if item.group == 'devs' else '/sbin/nologin' }}"
        state: present
      loop: "{{ users }}"
```

**Verify:**

```bash
ansible all -m ansible.builtin.command -a "id ana" -b
ansible all -m ansible.builtin.command -a "getent passwd svcbot" -b   # /sbin/nologin
ansible-playbook users.yml            # run twice; second run changed=0
```

**Notes.** `append: true` is the module's `usermod -aG` — without it you replace the user's whole supplementary group list. The inline conditional expression keeps this to one task; a `when:` with two separate tasks is equally correct if that reads more clearly to you. The `map`/`unique` filter chain derives the group list from the same data so it can't drift out of sync — a plain `loop: [devs, services]` is fine too.

If passwords are required, use `password: "{{ item.password | password_hash('sha512') }}"` with the values in Vault, and `no_log: true` on the task.

q: A playbook must run a legacy script /usr/local/bin/init-app.sh that has no module equivalent, exactly once per host, and must not report a change on subsequent runs.
a:
```yaml
- name: Initialise the application (once)
  ansible.builtin.command: /usr/local/bin/init-app.sh
  args:
    creates: /var/lib/app/.initialised
  become: true
```

If the script doesn't create a marker of its own, make one — and be explicit about what a change means:

```yaml
- name: Initialise the application (once)
  ansible.builtin.command: /usr/local/bin/init-app.sh
  args:
    creates: /var/lib/app/.initialised
  register: init
  become: true

- name: Record that initialisation happened
  ansible.builtin.file:
    path: /var/lib/app/.initialised
    state: touch
    mode: '0644'
  when: init is changed
  become: true
```

**Verify:**

```bash
ansible-playbook init.yml     # first run: changed
ansible-playbook init.yml     # second run: "skipped" — changed=0
```

**The principle.** `command` and `shell` report `changed` on every run because Ansible has no way to know what they did. `creates:` (skip if this path exists) and `removes:` (skip if it doesn't) are the built-in answers; `changed_when:` is the answer when the script's *exit code or output* tells you whether it acted — e.g. `changed_when: init.rc == 2`.

Before writing either, spend fifteen seconds on `ansible-doc -l | grep <thing>`: a real module usually exists, and it comes with idempotency for free.

q: Generate /etc/hosts.allow-servers on every host, listing the IP address of every machine in the webservers group, one per line as IP hostname.
a:
**`templates/servers.j2`:**

```jinja
# Managed by Ansible — do not edit by hand
{% for host in groups['webservers'] %}
{{ hostvars[host]['ansible_facts']['default_ipv4']['address'] }}  {{ hostvars[host]['ansible_facts']['fqdn'] }}
{% endfor %}
```

**The play:**

```yaml
---
- name: Distribute the server list
  hosts: all
  become: true
  tasks:
    - name: Deploy the list
      ansible.builtin.template:
        src: servers.j2
        dest: /etc/hosts.allow-servers
        owner: root
        group: root
        mode: '0644'
```

**Verify:**

```bash
ansible-playbook servers.yml --check --diff     # see the rendered text first
ansible all -m ansible.builtin.command -a "cat /etc/hosts.allow-servers"
ansible-playbook servers.yml                    # then twice, for changed=0
```

**The pattern being tested** is `groups[...]` plus `hostvars[...]` — the standard way to generate configuration on one host that describes *other* hosts, exactly as you would for a load balancer or cluster member list.

**One caveat worth knowing:** `hostvars[...]['ansible_facts']` is only populated for hosts whose facts have been gathered in this run. If the play targets only `dbservers` but the template reads facts of `webservers`, add a preliminary play (`hosts: webservers, gather_facts: true`) or use `ansible.builtin.setup` against them first.

q: Ensure PermitRootLogin no is set in /etc/ssh/sshd_config on every host, without replacing the rest of the file, and restart sshd only when it actually changes. A broken config must never be installed.
a:
```yaml
---
- name: Harden sshd
  hosts: all
  become: true

  tasks:
    - name: Disable root login
      ansible.builtin.lineinfile:
        path: /etc/ssh/sshd_config
        regexp: '^\s*#?\s*PermitRootLogin'
        line: 'PermitRootLogin no'
        state: present
        validate: '/usr/sbin/sshd -t -f %s'
      notify: Restart sshd

  handlers:
    - name: Restart sshd
      ansible.builtin.service:
        name: sshd
        state: restarted
```

**Verify:**

```bash
ansible-playbook sshd.yml --check --diff
ansible all -m ansible.builtin.command -a "grep -E '^PermitRootLogin' /etc/ssh/sshd_config" -b
ansible-playbook sshd.yml         # twice; second run changed=0, no restart
```

**Three details.** The **`regexp:`** is what makes this idempotent *and* what lets it fix an existing commented-out or differently-valued line rather than appending a duplicate — matching the commented form (`#?`) is deliberate. **`validate:`** runs `sshd -t` against a temp copy and refuses to install a file that fails, which is the difference between a typo and losing SSH access to every managed host. And the **handler** means sshd restarts only where the line actually changed.

**When to stop using `lineinfile`:** if the task grew to four or five settings in the same file, switch to a `template` and own the whole file — several `lineinfile` tasks on one file is a smell.

q: A playbook needs a database password that must not be readable in the repository. Set it up so the playbook can run non-interactively.
a:
**Split the variables — readable names, encrypted values:**

```bash
mkdir -p group_vars/dbservers
ansible-vault create group_vars/dbservers/vault.yml
```

```yaml
# group_vars/dbservers/vault.yml  (encrypted)
---
vault_db_password: S3cret!Passw0rd
```

```yaml
# group_vars/dbservers/vars.yml  (plaintext, reviewable)
---
db_password: "{{ vault_db_password }}"
```

**Non-interactive runs:**

```bash
echo 'my-vault-password' > ~/.vault_pass
chmod 600 ~/.vault_pass
```

```ini
# ansible.cfg
[defaults]
vault_password_file = ~/.vault_pass
```

**Use it, without leaking it:**

```yaml
- name: Set the database password
  ansible.builtin.user:
    name: dbadmin
    password: "{{ db_password | password_hash('sha512') }}"
  no_log: true
```

**Verify:**

```bash
ansible-vault view group_vars/dbservers/vault.yml     # readable with the password
head -1 group_vars/dbservers/vault.yml                # $ANSIBLE_VAULT;1.1;AES256
ansible-playbook db.yml                               # runs without prompting
```

**The three things being tested.** The file is genuinely encrypted (check the header). The password file is `chmod 600` and never committed — an encrypted vault beside a world-readable password achieves nothing. And `no_log: true` keeps the secret out of the run output, which is otherwise a very easy place to leak it.

**Alternative:** for a single value in an otherwise fine file, `ansible-vault encrypt_string 'S3cret!' --name 'db_password'` and paste the output in. `--ask-vault-pass` replaces the password file when a prompt is acceptable.

q: Create a role apache in the project's roles/ directory that installs httpd, deploys a templated index.html, opens the firewall, and restarts httpd on config change. The document root and port must be overridable.
a:
```bash cd /home/ansible/project ansible-galaxy init roles/apache ``` ```yaml # roles/apache/defaults/main.yml <- overridable, because defaults lose to everything --- http_port: 80 doc_root: /var/www/html ``` ```yaml # roles/apache/tasks/main.yml --- - name: Install httpd ansible.builtin.dnf: name: httpd state: present - name: Deploy the home page ansible.builtin.template: src: index.html.j2 dest: "{{ doc_root }}/index.html" owner: root group: root mode: '0644' notify: Restart httpd - name: Open the firewall ansible.posix.firewalld: port: "{{ http_port }}/tcp" state: enabled permanent: true immediate: true - name: Start and enable httpd ansible.builtin.service: name: httpd state: started enabled: true ``` ```yaml # roles/apache/handlers/main.yml --- - name: Restart httpd ansible.builtin.service: name: httpd state: restarted ``` ```jinja {# roles/apache/templates/index.html.j2 #}

{{ ansible_facts['fqdn'] }} — port {{ http_port }}

``` **Use it, with an override:** ```yaml --- - hosts: webservers become: true roles: - role: apache vars: http_port: 8080 ``` **Verify:** ```bash ansible-playbook site.yml ansible-playbook site.yml # changed=0 ansible webservers -m ansible.builtin.command -a "curl -s http://localhost:8080/" -b ``` **The design point:** `http_port` and `doc_root` go in **`defaults/`**, not `vars/`. Defaults have the lowest precedence of any source, which is exactly what makes them overridable from the play, `group_vars`, or `-e`. A value in `vars/main.yml` would resist all of that — and that's the usual reason a role appears to ignore a variable someone set.

q: Configure time synchronisation against time.example.com on all hosts using a RHEL system role, and install the project's required collections from requirements.yml into the project directory.
a:
**Find the role and read its interface first — this is the actual skill:**

```bash
dnf install -y rhel-system-roles
ls /usr/share/ansible/roles/
ls /usr/share/doc/rhel-system-roles/timesync/     # README + example playbooks
ansible-galaxy collection list | grep rhel_system_roles
```

**The playbook:**

```yaml
---
- name: Configure time synchronisation
  hosts: all
  become: true
  vars:
    timesync_ntp_servers:
      - hostname: time.example.com
        iburst: true
  roles:
    - redhat.rhel_system_roles.timesync
```

**The requirements file and a project-local install:**

```yaml
# requirements.yml
---
collections:
  - name: ansible.posix
  - name: community.general
```

```bash
ansible-galaxy collection install -r requirements.yml -p collections/
```

```ini
# ansible.cfg
[defaults]
collections_path = ./collections
roles_path       = ./roles
```

**Verify:**

```bash
ansible-playbook timesync.yml
ansible-playbook timesync.yml                       # changed=0
ansible all -m ansible.builtin.command -a "chronyc sources" -b
ansible-galaxy collection list                      # from ./collections
```

**How to approach any system role:** you don't read its tasks — you read `/usr/share/doc/rhel-system-roles/<role>/` for the **variables** it accepts and copy the example playbook it ships. That directory is the highest-value thing on the machine when a task names a system role.

**Version note:** depending on what's installed, the role may be addressed as `redhat.rhel_system_roles.timesync` or as plain `rhel-system-roles.timesync`. Check `ls /usr/share/ansible/roles/` and `ansible-galaxy collection list` on the machine and use what's actually there. On an offline exam, collections install from a local path or URL the task provides — same command, different source.

q: On dbservers, create a volume group vg_data on /dev/vdb, a 2 GiB logical volume lv_app formatted XFS, mounted at /data and persistent across reboots — all with Ansible.
a:
```yaml
---
- name: Provision application storage
  hosts: dbservers
  become: true

  tasks:
    - name: Partition the disk
      community.general.parted:
        device: /dev/vdb
        number: 1
        state: present
        part_end: 2GiB
        flags: [ lvm ]

    - name: Create the volume group
      community.general.lvg:
        vg: vg_data
        pvs: /dev/vdb1

    - name: Create the logical volume
      community.general.lvol:
        vg: vg_data
        lv: lv_app
        size: 2g

    - name: Create the filesystem
      community.general.filesystem:
        fstype: xfs
        dev: /dev/vg_data/lv_app

    - name: Mount it and write it to fstab
      ansible.posix.mount:
        path: /data
        src: /dev/vg_data/lv_app
        fstype: xfs
        opts: defaults
        state: mounted
```

**Verify:**

```bash
ansible-playbook storage.yml
ansible-playbook storage.yml                                    # changed=0
ansible dbservers -m ansible.builtin.command -a "df -h /data" -b
ansible dbservers -m ansible.builtin.command -a "grep /data /etc/fstab" -b
```

**`state: mounted` is the whole persistence answer** — it mounts now *and* writes the fstab entry. `present` would only write fstab (no mount); `absent` removes both. That single parameter is the RHCSA lesson about `mount` versus `/etc/fstab`, encoded.

**Growing it later** is `community.general.lvol` with `size: +1g` and `resizefs: true` — the module's `lvextend -r`, filesystem included.

⚠️ Storage playbooks are destructive. Run against a scratch host first, and confirm the device name with `ansible dbservers -m ansible.builtin.setup -a "filter=ansible_devices"` rather than assuming `/dev/vdb`.

q: Configure a local-extras repository on all hosts, install nmap from it, and schedule /usr/local/bin/report.sh to run as ana at 06:15 on weekdays.
a:
```yaml
---
- name: Software and scheduling
  hosts: all
  become: true

  tasks:
    - name: Configure the repository
      ansible.builtin.yum_repository:
        name: local-extras
        description: Local Extras
        baseurl: http://server.example.com/extras/
        enabled: true
        gpgcheck: false

    - name: Install nmap
      ansible.builtin.dnf:
        name: nmap
        state: present

    - name: Schedule the report
      ansible.builtin.cron:
        name: "daily report"
        user: ana
        minute: "15"
        hour: "6"
        weekday: "1-5"
        job: "/usr/local/bin/report.sh"
```

**Verify:**

```bash
ansible-playbook software.yml
ansible-playbook software.yml                                        # changed=0
ansible all -m ansible.builtin.command -a "rpm -q nmap"
ansible all -m ansible.builtin.command -a "crontab -l -u ana" -b
```

**Two idempotency details.** `state: present` rather than `latest` — `latest` reports `changed` whenever an upgrade exists upstream, so your second run is never clean. And the cron entry's **`name:`** is its identity: Ansible writes it as a comment and uses it to find and update the job later, so changing the schedule updates the entry instead of adding a duplicate.

`yum_repository` writes `/etc/yum.repos.d/local-extras.repo` for you — no template needed. If the task supplies a GPG key, set `gpgcheck: true` and `gpgkey:` rather than disabling the check.

q: Apache must serve from /web on port 8888 on the webservers group, with SELinux left enforcing.
a:
```yaml
---
- name: Apache on a non-standard root and port
  hosts: webservers
  become: true

  tasks:
    - name: Install httpd
      ansible.builtin.dnf:
        name: httpd
        state: present

    - name: Create the document root
      ansible.builtin.file:
        path: /web
        state: directory
        owner: root
        group: root
        mode: '0755'

    - name: Label the directory for httpd
      community.general.sefcontext:
        target: '/web(/.*)?'
        setype: httpd_sys_content_t
        state: present
      notify: Restore contexts

    - name: Label the port for httpd
      community.general.seport:
        ports: '8888'
        proto: tcp
        setype: http_port_t
        state: present

    - name: Configure httpd
      ansible.builtin.template:
        src: httpd.conf.j2
        dest: /etc/httpd/conf/httpd.conf
        mode: '0644'
      notify: Restart httpd

    - name: Open the firewall
      ansible.posix.firewalld:
        port: 8888/tcp
        state: enabled
        permanent: true
        immediate: true

    - name: Start and enable httpd
      ansible.builtin.service:
        name: httpd
        state: started
        enabled: true

  handlers:
    - name: Restore contexts
      ansible.builtin.command: restorecon -Rv /web
      changed_when: false

    - name: Restart httpd
      ansible.builtin.service:
        name: httpd
        state: restarted
```

**Verify:**

```bash
ansible-playbook web8888.yml
ansible-playbook web8888.yml                                     # changed=0
ansible webservers -m ansible.builtin.command -a "curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' http://localhost:8888/" -b
ansible webservers -m ansible.builtin.command -a "ausearch -m AVC -ts recent" -b   # quiet
```

**Why three SELinux-adjacent steps.** The **directory** needs the right file context, the **port** needs to carry `http_port_t` before httpd may bind it, and the firewall needs opening — the same three things you'd do by hand, and the same three that get forgotten. `sefcontext` records the rule but doesn't relabel existing files, which is why the `restorecon` handler exists; `changed_when: false` on it keeps re-runs clean.

If `community.general.seport` isn't available in your environment, `ansible.builtin.command: semanage port -a -t http_port_t -p tcp 8888` with a suitable `changed_when`/`creates`-style guard is an acceptable fallback — but check for the module first.

q: Your playbook reports changed=2 on every run even though the systems are already in the desired state. Diagnose and fix it.
a:
**Find which tasks:**

```bash
ansible-playbook site.yml --diff       # shows WHAT changed for file/template tasks
ansible-playbook site.yml -v           # per-task results
```

**The usual culprits, in order of likelihood:**

| Cause | Fix |
|---|---|
| A `command`/`shell` task that only reads state | `changed_when: false` |
| A `command`/`shell` that acts but has no marker | `args: creates: /path/to/marker`, or `changed_when: result.rc == 2` |
| `dnf` with `state: latest` | `state: present` unless upgrades are actually required |
| `lineinfile` without `regexp:` | Add `regexp:` so it replaces rather than appends |
| A template rendering differently each run (a timestamp!) | Remove the volatile value, or exclude it from the file |
| `file` with `state: touch` | Use `state: file` or guard it with `when:` |

```yaml
- name: Read-only check — never a change
  ansible.builtin.command: systemctl is-active httpd
  register: svc
  changed_when: false
  failed_when: false
```

**Verify the fix the same way you verify a task:**

```bash
ansible-playbook site.yml
ansible-playbook site.yml       # PLAY RECAP must show changed=0
```

**Why this matters beyond tidiness:** a task that always reports `changed` also always fires its **handlers**, so a service gets restarted on every run. On a real system that's an outage you scheduled by accident — which is why idempotency is treated as correctness rather than style.

q: A deployment task must roll back to a known-good config and log the attempt if the new configuration fails validation or the service won't restart.
a:
```yaml
---
- name: Deploy with rollback
  hosts: appservers
  become: true

  tasks:
    - name: Deploy, and recover if it fails
      block:
        - name: Install the new configuration
          ansible.builtin.template:
            src: app.conf.j2
            dest: /etc/app/app.conf
            mode: '0644'
            backup: true
            validate: '/usr/bin/app --test -c %s'

        - name: Restart the application
          ansible.builtin.service:
            name: app
            state: restarted

      rescue:
        - name: Restore the known-good configuration
          ansible.builtin.copy:
            src: files/app.conf.known-good
            dest: /etc/app/app.conf
            mode: '0644'

        - name: Restart with the restored configuration
          ansible.builtin.service:
            name: app
            state: restarted

        - name: Make the failure visible
          ansible.builtin.debug:
            msg: "Deployment failed on {{ inventory_hostname }} — rolled back"

      always:
        - name: Log the attempt
          ansible.builtin.lineinfile:
            path: /var/log/deploy.log
            line: "{{ ansible_date_time.iso8601 }} deploy attempted on {{ inventory_hostname }}"
            create: true
            mode: '0644'
```

**Verify by breaking it on purpose:**

```bash
ansible-playbook deploy.yml --check --diff        # preview the rendered config
# then deliberately break app.conf.j2 and re-run — the rescue block should fire
ansible appservers -m ansible.builtin.command -a "tail -3 /var/log/deploy.log" -b
```

**What each part buys you.** `validate:` catches a bad config *before* it's installed, so most failures never reach the rescue block at all. `backup: true` keeps a timestamped copy of the previous file on the host. `rescue` runs only when something in the block failed; `always` runs either way, which is what makes the log honest.

⚠️ Note that the `always` block appends a line on every run, so this play is deliberately **not** `changed=0` on a second run — that's correct here (a log entry is the point), but it's worth recognising that you've made that trade on purpose rather than by accident.

q: Deploy a new application version to the webservers group one host at a time, removing each host from the load balancer (lb1.example.com) before the change and adding it back afterwards. The rollout must stop entirely if any host fails.
a:
```yaml
---
- name: Rolling deployment
  hosts: webservers
  become: true
  serial: 1
  max_fail_percentage: 0

  tasks:
    - name: Drain this host from the load balancer
      ansible.builtin.command: /usr/local/bin/lb-drain {{ inventory_hostname }}
      delegate_to: lb1.example.com
      changed_when: true

    - name: Deploy the application
      ansible.builtin.dnf:
        name: myapp
        state: latest
      notify: Restart myapp

    - name: Apply pending restarts before we re-enable traffic
      ansible.builtin.meta: flush_handlers

    - name: Wait for the app to answer locally
      ansible.builtin.uri:
        url: http://localhost:8080/health
        status_code: 200
      retries: 12
      delay: 5
      register: health
      until: health.status == 200

    - name: Return this host to the load balancer
      ansible.builtin.command: /usr/local/bin/lb-enable {{ inventory_hostname }}
      delegate_to: lb1.example.com
      changed_when: true

  handlers:
    - name: Restart myapp
      ansible.builtin.service:
        name: myapp
        state: restarted
```

**Verify:**

```bash
ansible-playbook rollout.yml --limit web1        # canary a single host first
ansible-playbook rollout.yml
```

**The three keywords doing the work.** `serial: 1` runs the *whole play* on one host before moving to the next — that's a rolling update, and it's different from `forks`, which only limits concurrency within a single task. `delegate_to: lb1.example.com` runs the drain/enable **on the load balancer** while `{{ inventory_hostname }}` still refers to the web server being worked on. `max_fail_percentage: 0` stops the rollout at the first failure instead of breaking every host in sequence.

`meta: flush_handlers` matters here: handlers normally run at the very end of the play, which would put the host back in the load balancer *before* the restart. Forcing them early keeps the order honest.

⚠️ This play is deliberately not `changed=0` on a second run — the drain/enable commands have no natural idempotency, hence the explicit `changed_when: true`. Where a real load-balancer module exists, prefer it.

q: A playbook must apply all available updates and reboot each host if the kernel changed, then wait for it to come back. A separate 30-minute reindex job must be started without holding up the play.
a:
```yaml
---
- name: Patch and reindex
  hosts: all
  become: true

  tasks:
    - name: Apply all updates
      ansible.builtin.dnf:
        name: "*"
        state: latest
      register: updates

    - name: Check whether a reboot is required
      ansible.builtin.command: needs-restarting -r
      register: restart_check
      failed_when: false
      changed_when: false

    - name: Reboot if needed, and wait for the host to return
      ansible.builtin.reboot:
        reboot_timeout: 600
        msg: "Rebooting after package updates"
      when: restart_check.rc != 0

    - name: Start the reindex and move on
      ansible.builtin.command: /usr/local/bin/reindex.sh
      async: 1800
      poll: 0
      register: reindex

    - name: ...other work happens here while it runs...
      ansible.builtin.debug:
        msg: "Reindex started as job {{ reindex.ansible_job_id }}"

    - name: Collect the reindex result
      ansible.builtin.async_status:
        jid: "{{ reindex.ansible_job_id }}"
      register: reindex_result
      until: reindex_result.finished
      retries: 60
      delay: 30
```

**Verify:**

```bash
ansible-playbook patch.yml --limit web1
ansible all -m ansible.builtin.command -a "uptime"
```

**Why each piece.** `ansible.builtin.reboot` exists because `command: reboot` fails — the connection dies before the module can report success. The module expects the disconnection and returns only once the host answers again (`wait_for_connection` does the waiting half if something else triggered the reboot).

**`async: 1800` with `poll: 0`** is fire-and-forget: the job starts, the play continues immediately, and the SSH connection isn't held open for half an hour (which is what causes the timeout failures people hit on long tasks). `async_status` with the registered `ansible_job_id` plus `until: … .finished` collects the result later. With `poll: <n>` instead of 0, Ansible waits but polls rather than holding the connection.

`needs-restarting -r` exits non-zero when a reboot is required — hence `failed_when: false` (a non-zero exit is *information* here) and `changed_when: false` (it's a read-only check, and without this the play never reaches a clean second run).
